finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id never awaits authorize(), so the delete runs regardless of the grant check. Any caller can delete any report, including callers with no grant and, because nothing guards req.user, callers with no session user.
finding.source: Any HTTP request to DELETE /reports/:id with any report id. No guard runs before line 20.

trace.note: report loaded by req.params.id with no owner/tenant check
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returns a pending promise and the handler continues
inside authorize, db.grants is awaited, so control returns to the handler before the check finishes
the 403 path is reached only after the handler has already moved on
throw becomes a rejected promise that nothing handles

finding.guards_checked: The grant check exists in authorize() but is not enforced: the call is not awaited and the rejection is not caught (Express 4 does not catch rejections from async handlers). No route-level or global auth middleware is visible in this file. If req.user is undefined, user.id throws inside authorize, which is the same unhandled path, so the delete still proceeds.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only grant check is authorize() (server.js:9-16), which is called without await at server.js:20, so its throw at line 14 becomes an unhandled rejection and the handler proceeds to db.reports.remove at line 21. The only middleware (server.js:4-7) just copies req.session.user onto req.user and enforces nothing. No route-level or global auth is visible in this file. Contrast PUT at server.js:27, which does await authorize().
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the grant check at server.js:11-14 cannot stop the unconditional db.reports.remove at server.js:21, and no visible auth middleware (server.js:4-7) gates the route. Caveat: the anonymous case assumes no auth is applied outside this file; if req.session is undefined, line 5 throws synchronously and the request returns 500 before any delete. The unhandled rejection from line 14 will also crash a Node 15+ process by default, a separate availability impact.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update, so a caller with 'write' on a report can set any column, including ownership or tenant fields if the schema has them.
finding.source: req.body on PUT /reports/:id (express.json() at line 3); attacker holds a 'write' grant on the report.

trace.note: express.json() parses the body into req.body with no field allowlist
whole req.body is forwarded to update with no field filter

finding.guards_checked: The per-object 'write' grant is checked and awaited. Nothing restricts which fields can be written. The db layer is not in the repo, so whether owner_id, tenant_id, or similar columns exist, and whether the db layer filters them, is unknown. Confidence is medium until the schema is checked.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is awaited and throws a 403 when the grant is missing (server.js:9-16), so only callers holding a 'write' grant on the report reach line 28. No field allowlist or filter exists in server.js. Whether the db.reports.update layer filters columns is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: express.json() at server.js:3 feeds req.body, the awaited write check at server.js:27 gates the call, and server.js:28 forwards the whole body unfiltered. Whether this is an escalation depends on whether the reports schema has ownership or tenant columns and whether the uncommitted db layer filters them, and neither is in the repo, so the impact cannot be decided from the code available.
